segments: [page 187] the Romans for nine days, laying waste.
And when they were wanting to depart,
the sister's son of Emperor Romanos, who was with Nicephorus, argued and said,
"We will not depart until we take the fortress."
Nicephorus, however, because he was not able to oppose him, said,
"Behold, the fortress is before you;
go, conquer it."
And when that nephew of the emperor approached the gate of the fortress,
they cast a stone upon him from the loophole that was above the gate.
And when the stone struck him,
he turned his face to flee.
The people inside opened the gate of the fortress,
and a certain Daylamite named Basha pursued him,
and struck him with a lance between his shoulders,
and it came out through his chest, and he killed him.
Those who were with him, however, turned back,
lifted up his corpse, and carried it to Nicephorus.
He, then, in order to avenge the blood of the emperor's nephew,
cut off the heads of one thousand and two hundred Arab men who were bound with him,
and set off and went to the land of the Romans.
In the villages of Aleppo, however, he did not destroy anything at all,
but commanded the farmers:
"Do not neglect the cultivation of the lands,
because this territory belongs to us,
and after a little while we will return to you."
At that same time, again, a thousand Armenian foot-soldiers came against the territory of Edessa,
and took captive a thousand sheep, five hundred oxen, and ten Arab men, and departed.
In these times, when the Romans gained strength over the Arabs,
and raided and reached as far as Greater Armenia,
and left and went on,
the children of Armenia,
because they were afraid of the Arabs lest they take vengeance on them because they were Christians,
all fled to the territory of the Romans.
And the Romans gave them Sebasteia of Cappadocia,
and they multiplied there greatly.
And they also settled them in those fortresses in Cilicia that they had taken from the Arabs.
And in all the battles,
Armenian foot-soldiers also used to go with the Romans,
and they were very successful.
And when Nicephorus with the Roman forces returned from Aleppo and reached Simnadu {Synnada?},
news of the death of Emperor Romanos reached them.
And all the generals agreed in one counsel with Tzimiskes,
and proclaimed Nicephorus the Domesticus emperor in the year 1275
of the Greeks [964 AD].
